subtype: Approach: asking for the whole amount as a birthday gift [Thinking]
passage:
Early October. Vaibhav wrote on the back of his hand: Diwali = money? He thought it over. Gifts from relatives were always books or clothes, but money could buy the game console he wanted. He decided to ask for cash this year and keep his pocket money in the tin as well.

Diwali evening. Bua Preeti pressed an envelope into his palm. Two other relatives gave him sweets and clothes.

The day after. Vaibhav counted: the envelope was helpful, but not enough on its own. He put it in the tin beside his weekly coins. "Good thing I kept saving," he thought.

qa.q: Who gave Vaibhav an envelope on Diwali evening?
qa.a: Bua Preeti gave Vaibhav an envelope.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav think when he counted the money the day after Diwali?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt relieved he had kept saving, since the envelope helped but was not enough by itself.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Vaibhav use to reach the amount, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could earn extra through small jobs at home or set a smaller first target. These do not depend on other people, so the goal stays in his own hands.

qa.q: How might the relatives see a request for money instead of a gift?
qa.a: Two relatives still gave sweets and clothes, so some may prefer to choose a present themselves, while Bua Preeti was happy to give cash.

grounding: A boy decides to ask relatives for money at Diwali instead of gifts, which is a shortcut that depends on others, so he keeps saving as well.

subtype: Approach: giving up when the goal seems too far [Pitfall]
passage: After two weeks of dropping coins in the jar, Chaitanya looked at the total and sighed. Only Rs 90. The remote-control car cost Rs 600. "That will take forever," he told Avni at recess. "Then why not buy something else?" Avni said, shrugging. That evening Chaitanya broke the jar and bought a cheap plastic car from the corner stall. It looked good for a day. On the third day, one wheel fell off and the steering stopped working. He sat with the broken toy in his hands, the jar empty, the money gone, and the real car further away than ever.

qa.q: How much money did Chaitanya have after two weeks?
qa.a: Chaitanya had Rs 90 after two weeks.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he decided to break the jar?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt discouraged and impatient, because the goal seemed too far away and he wanted something now. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Chaitanya use, and why?
qa.a: Chaitanya could set a smaller first target and mark each step, because shorter goals feel reachable. Asking a parent for a way to earn extra could also help.

qa.q: How might Avni see the choice to buy the cheap car?
qa.a: Avni suggested buying something else and shrugged, so Avni may not have realised how much the savings and the goal mattered to Chaitanya.

grounding: After two weeks a boy decides that 600 rupees will take too long, spends the savings on a cheap toy that breaks and ends up with less than planned.

subtype: Approach: setting a smaller first target [Revision]
passage:
Mohit: Alka didi, the jar has Rs 130. The car is Rs 600. I'm never going to get there.
Alka: You started two weeks ago, chhote bhai. Are you giving up?
Mohit: I feel like it. It's too big.
Alka: What if the goal was smaller? Just for now.
Mohit: Like what?
Alka: Rs 200. You're already past half of that.
Mohit: Rs 200... that's only three more weeks.
Alka: Right. Then celebrate, and set the next one.
Three weeks later, Mohit reached Rs 200, ran to Mummy and yelled, "I did it!" They shared a kulfi.

qa.q: How much was in Mohit's jar when he spoke to Alka?
qa.a: There was Rs 130 in the jar.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when saying the goal was too big?
qa.a: Mohit felt discouraged and close to giving up, since Rs 600 seemed impossible to reach from Rs 130. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Mohit use later to keep going, and why?
qa.a: Mohit could mark each Rs 100 on a chart or earn extra through a job at home. Seeing progress or shortening the wait keeps patience alive.

qa.q: How does Alka's suggestion affect Mohit's mood?
qa.a: Alka's smaller goal makes the target feel possible, so Mohit's mood lifts from discouraged to excited, shown by running to Mummy and yelling.

grounding: Noticing he feels discouraged, the boy sets a first goal of Rs 200, celebrates when he reaches it and carries on toward the full price.

subtype: Approach: changing her mind after thinking again about the want [Revision]
passage: Tuition teacher's note. Ayesha has been putting aside her pocket money for six weeks to buy a toy castle. Today at the shop window she stopped and stood for a long time. "Will I still play with it in a month?" she said quietly. She looked at the picture of the castle stuck on her notebook cover. After some thought she told me, "I think a book series and an art set will last longer." She crossed out the castle and wrote two new lines. I did not push her either way. She seemed calm about it, and took her time. Kalyani, tuition teacher.

qa.q: How long had Ayesha been saving?
qa.a: Ayesha had been saving for six weeks.

qa.q: What did Ayesha think about at the shop window, and what does it show about her wants?
qa.a: Ayesha thought about whether she would still want the castle in a month, which shows she was thinking carefully instead of only wanting it now.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ayesha use to test the want, and why?
qa.a: Ayesha could wait another week and see if she still wants it, or ask a friend how long they played with theirs. Time shows whether a want lasts.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Ayesha's choice?
qa.a: Kalyani watched and chose not to push, so Kalyani sees a child making a calm, thoughtful choice without a grown-up steering it.

grounding: After saving for six weeks, a girl asks herself if she will still play with the toy in a month and decides a book series and art set are a better use of the money.

subtype: Approach: breaking cleaning his room into small jobs [Thinking]
passage: I'm Gautam. Last Sunday my room looked as if a storm had passed. Socks on the fan, comics under the chair, cars in a heap. I stood at the door and wanted to go back to bed. Then I said to myself: one thing at a time. First just clothes, all the clothes, into the cupboard or the basket. Done. Then books, on the shelf. Then toys, in the box. Last, the floor, with the broom. Each time I finished a part, the mess got smaller. After forty minutes, Nitin looked in and said, "Who cleaned this?" I said, "Me, one bit at a time."

qa.q: What did Gautam do first when cleaning?
qa.a: Gautam put the clothes in the cupboard or the basket first.

qa.q: What did Gautam feel at the door of the messy room?
qa.a: Gautam felt overwhelmed and wanted to go back to bed, until splitting the job into parts made it seem smaller.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Gautam use, and why?
qa.a: Gautam could put everything on the bed and sort it into piles, or race a timer. Both make the job clearer or more fun, so it feels less heavy.

qa.q: How might Nitin see the tidy room?
qa.a: Nitin looked in and asked who had cleaned, so Nitin was surprised and probably impressed that the storm-hit room was neat.

grounding: A boy overwhelmed by a messy room splits it into clothes, books, toys and floor and does one at a time, so the mess shrinks with each finished part.

subtype: Approach: putting everything on the bed then sorting it [Action]
passage: Navya's room looked like a market after closing time. She sighed, then pulled the bedspread flat and started scooping. Everything on the floor went onto the bed: notebooks, a dupatta, a broken hairband, half a mango peel, coloured pencils. Her brother Jomon peeked in. "That's worse!" "Wait," said Navya. Now she could see it all. She made three piles: things for the cupboard, things for the shelf, things for the bin. The mango peel and hairband went into the bin, pencils to the shelf, the dupatta to the cupboard. Ten minutes later the bed was clear and the floor shone. Jomon just grinned.

qa.q: Where did Navya put everything from the floor first?
qa.a: Navya put everything from the floor onto the bed.

qa.q: How does Navya seem to feel when starting on the room?
qa.a: Navya sighed at first, so the mess felt heavy, but calm scooping and sorting suggest she grew more confident.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Navya use, and why?
qa.a: Navya could tackle one type of item at a time, such as books first and then clothes. That splits the mess into smaller jobs that are easy to finish.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Navya's method at the start?
qa.a: Jomon said 'That's worse!' when the bed was piled high, so Jomon first saw a bigger mess, until the piles showed the plan.

grounding: A girl puts everything from the floor on the bed and sorts it into piles for the cupboard, the shelf and the bin, so choices become easier.

subtype: Approach: stuffing things under the bed to look clean [Pitfall]
passage: The hostel's Sunday visiting hour began at four, and Chirag's mother was already on the stairs. He grabbed the mess on his side of the room, shirts, an old lunch box, a pile of notebooks, and shoved them under the bed. The dorm looked neat. Dishant, on the next bed, raised an eyebrow but said nothing. His mother nodded at the room and smiled, and Chirag felt clever. On Monday at half past seven the bell rang for assembly. Chirag dropped to his knees, digging under the bed, but his school shoes were somewhere in the heap. He was late and the warden noticed. The mess was still there.

qa.q: When did visiting hour begin at the hostel?
qa.a: The visiting hour began at four.

qa.q: How did Chirag feel when his mother smiled at the neat room, and how did that change on Monday?
qa.a: Chirag felt clever, but on Monday he probably felt flustered and worried while digging for the shoes.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Chirag use, and why?
qa.a: Chirag could sort things into their places in five minutes, or make one pile to sort later. Then the room would look neat and things would still be findable.

qa.q: How might Dishant see Chirag's quick clean-up?
qa.a: Dishant raised an eyebrow and said nothing, so Dishant probably doubted the plan but chose not to argue with Chirag, who was in a hurry.

grounding: A boy hides clutter under the bed to satisfy his mother quickly, and the room looks neat but next day he cannot find his school shoes.

subtype: Approach: racing the clock to make it a game [Thinking]
passage: Note from Raghav's mother, Rekha. I watched my son's room-cleaning trick tonight. He set the kitchen timer to ten minutes and announced, "Yesterday I took eleven. Today I beat it." He said to me, "If it's a race, I don't get bored. I just keep going." The timer ticked, and he threw clothes into the basket, stacked books, and slid the toys into the box. He was breathing hard and grinning when the bell rang, with one minute left over. I had not asked him to hurry, only to tidy. Turning it into a game was his own idea.

qa.q: How long did Raghav set the timer for?
qa.a: Raghav set the timer for ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Raghav think about turning the chore into a race?
qa.a: Raghav thinks a race keeps him from getting bored so he can keep going, which shows he enjoys the challenge. 😊

qa.q: What alternative approach could Raghav use if racing stops being fun, and why?
qa.a: Raghav could play a favourite song and finish before it ends, or split the room into small jobs. A new challenge would keep his attention on the job.

qa.q: How does Rekha see her son's method?
qa.a: Rekha had only asked him to tidy, so she sees a child who found his own way and is pleased and a little surprised.

grounding: A boy sets a ten-minute timer and tries to beat yesterday's time, making the chore a race so he stays focused and has fun.

subtype: Approach: making a chore chart with turns among siblings [Action]
passage: Hafsa, when I was small we were three children in the house, and every evening the same fight: who laid the table, who swept, who watered the plants. So one Sunday I, Tenzin, took a big sheet of paper. We wrote the chores across the top and our three names down the side, then drew arrows so the names moved one place each week. Pinned on the kitchen door, everyone could see whose turn it was. I liked it because nobody had to say 'You always do less'. The fight faded, though my brother still forgot the plants now and then, and we laughed at that.

qa.q: Where was the chore chart pinned?
qa.a: The chart was pinned on the kitchen door.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel about the chart in the kitchen?
qa.a: Tenzin liked it because nobody had to argue about who did less, which suggests a feeling of relief and fairness.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped end the fights, and why?
qa.a: Making the names move one place each week helped, because everyone did every chore and the turns were visible.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's brother have seen the chart?
qa.a: Tenzin's brother sometimes forgot the plants, and the group laughed about it, so the chart probably felt fair even when a turn was missed.

grounding: Three siblings write chores on a chart with rotating names so the sharing is open and nobody feels they do more than others.

subtype: Approach: complaining and delaying until asked five times [Pitfall]
passage: "Baljeet, please sweep the courtyard," said Papa from the cot. "Later," said Baljeet, looking at the wall. Ten minutes later: "Baljeet." "Later, Papa." By the fifth time, Papa's voice had gone tight. "I've asked five times!" "Why me? Wasim never sweeps!" Wasim watched from the doorway and said nothing. The argument went on until the sun was low. In the end Baljeet swept, and it took the same ten minutes it always took. But when she finished, the neighbour's television had already begun the cartoon, and the best part was over. She sat on the step, cross and silent.

qa.q: How many times did Papa ask Baljeet to sweep?
qa.a: Papa asked five times.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling at the end, sitting on the step?
qa.a: Baljeet was cross and probably regretful, since the sweeping took the usual ten minutes and the cartoon was missed.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Baljeet use next time, and why?
qa.a: Baljeet could sweep at once or choose a time, such as after tea, and tell Papa. A promise about when keeps the evening free and avoids the argument.

qa.q: How does Papa see Baljeet's 'later'?
qa.a: Papa asked again and again until the voice went tight, so Papa probably feels ignored and frustrated by having to repeat the request.

grounding: A girl keeps saying she will do it later, the delay becomes an argument, and the chore takes the same time while she loses her cartoon.
